speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture
speechtext:
Indeed, the hon. member for Joliette has many good farmers among his constituents. I had the opportunity to visit this constituency quite recently. I go there from time to time as I have some family in this beautiful region, and I am certain that the hon. member for Joliette, who will probably take the floor this afternoon, will also be proud to support the Canagrex bill because he also has chicken farmers, egg producers, dairy farmers and very good potato producers in his region. It is in this perspective, Mr. Speaker, that we want to support agriculture but not to eliminate surpluses, not at all, but we all know that, as I said earlier, our farmers are able to produce more and to double their production. We are a small nation of 25 million people and we are able to produce food to feed the world population, we can do our share to help developing countries or those that are still known as underdeveloped countries.
I too have had the opportunity in the last few months of travelling abroad, in places as far as Bangladesh, for instance, where, I can assure you, the only possible crop is rice. But other food products are needed: meat, milk and so on. Canada is a net exporter of dairy products, milk, powdered milk, condensed milk, butter, cheese, and grain. We want our western farmers to increase their grain production. We also have farmers who produce without land: they breed pigs; in fact we produce 140 per cent of what we need and therefore we are overproducing. We also have very good poultry and egg producers and so we are exporting. Canagrex will help small processing plants to find markets, Mr. Speaker. In the last few weeks, 1 had the opportunity of meeting representatives from Middle East countries who were visiting Canada; they were interested in buying Canadian farm products. We were asked if we had, like Mexico, an agency that would handle the trade because, as we know, some countries would rather trade on a country to country basis. Thus, Mr. Speaker, Canagrex will fill the void, the void between the processing plants or rather, the processors and potential buyers of Canadian products.
Mr. Speaker, a few years back when I was a member of the Quebec National Assembly I had a chance to speak on a somewhat similar bill under which the then government proposed to set up the SOQUIA Corporation. I can say that the Corporation is doing very useful work within Quebec. Certainly Canagrex would not have exactly as the same role as SOQUIA but the goals are almost identical, namely, to help first the farmers and second the processors. As far as I know, SOQUIA did not get very much involved in the export of
Canagrex Act
agricultural and food products. But surely with the co-operation of the provinces and of such a body as SOQUIA in Quebec, Canagrex will complete that network that is so important for the welfare of our Canadian agriculture.
In 1980, we had a $3.5 billion agri-food trade surplus, accounting for 75 per cent of the total Canadian trade surplus. In order to add to that positive tendency in our agricultural sector and enable Canada to meet the strong demand which is anticipated, the Department of Agriculture has adopted, as I stated earlier, an agri-food strategy based on three main aspects requiring co-operation and consultation. Those three aspects are most important, Mr. Speaker. First there is the processing of resources, second, the development of markets, and third, thematic agricultural research. Coming back to the processing of resources, we know that Canada must take into account the existing markets if we are to process the full range of our national resources through regional research and development. Farm production is affected by the policies of several federal departments. Further, the Canadian government and the provinces, as 1 said, share the responsibility for preserving and developing our resources. The provincial role is especially significant because the resources of this land and the advisory services fall within their jurisdiction. Consultation, liasion and co-operation within the federal government and with provinces are the key elements of that strategy. And in order to promote productive investments, the resource processing strategy must ensure technological progress through further research and the application of experimental results, combined with the necessary incentives.
Then there is the development of markets. The government has always contributed its effort to the development of better outlets for Canadian goods on foreign markets. During the last round of multilateral trade talks, Canada succeeded in reducing tariff barriers and securing for a great number of our Canadian farm products better access to foreign markets. Simultaneously, greater protection has been negotiated for part of our major garden crops. Thematic research is definitely an aspect that has always been a most vital concern of the Department of Agriculture, since more than $200 million are allocated to research in agri-food and agricultural research in Canada, but the Department of Agriculture will need more money to better promote that research. I would not say we are lagging behind, but we are not yet at the forefront as far as our research needs are concerned.
I have just highlighted a few aspects of that challenging strategy, but still it must rest on a structure which is both flexible and tailored to Canada's agricultural reality. Mr. Speaker, it is in that framework that the establishment of Canagrex gains its full significance. In a way, everything that has been done for the Canadian industry over the past ten years will be hallmarked today by the adoption of such an important bill. I am convinced that the Minister of Agriculture as well as hon. members on both sides of the House, whether

January 27, 1982
Canagrex Act
they spoke before or will speak after me, will explain the need for Canagrex as well as its objectives and its mandate. Personally, Mr. Speaker, during the few minutes at my disposal I would like to outline the make-up, the type of financing which the new corporation will be adopting.
First of all, the corporation will be headed by a chairman of the board and a president who will be his senior director, and an advisory committee to the Minister of Agriculture. The board of directors will set up its own subcommittees as required. During the first few years of Canagrex a team of monitors from the Agriculture Canada marketing and economics branch will be responsible for finding challenging marketing projects and taking a first look at the projects submitted by farmers, marketing agencies, co-operatives, provincial governments, processors or any other body related to the agricultural food sector.
The board of directors will have 11 members who, like its chairman, will be appointed by the governor in council upon the recommendation of the Minister of Agriculture. Most members will be selected among farmers known as leaders in their respective fields.
A moment earlier I heard the hon. member for Prince Albert say that farmers would not be appointed to the board of Canagrex. Not quite, because there will be farmers among the 11 appointed members. The board will also include spokesmen for the agricultural food industries and businessmen fully cognizant of export markets and experienced in banking, credit, insurance and foreign markets. It has also been proposed that the federal departments of agriculture and international trade be represented on the board which will be authorized to approve the projects. I heard my colleague opposite, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), say that he could not understand how Canagrex could possibly be connected with three different departments-agriculture, industry and commerce, and external affairs-and still manage to operate smoothly. I will explain to him. First, Agriculture Canada represents the agricultural community and the food processing industry. Second, Industry, Trade and Commerce represents the processing aspect of it, namely the manufacturing sector. Finally, External Affairs has a whole network of embassies throughout the world, and therefore Canagrex, through its board of directors, will dispatch its people to those embassies to work with their trade attaches to promote Canadian agricultural products. The hon. member for Elgin said something else which really surprised me, and I am quite sure that he did not really mean it. I quote from his speech of Monday last which can be found on page 14290 of Hansard:
How do we ensure the board of directors of Canagrex is composed of qualified people? These people are not around the country in great numbers.
I was taken aback by those remarks, because we do have good managers in this country, good experienced farmers, and good food processors. The hon. member for Elgin, the former
minister of Agriculture, tells us that qualified people in this country are not in great numbers.
And he said further and I quote:
It is extremely important that we secure well-qualified people, people who are ready to work and are capable of taking appropriate action.
I really do think the hon. member for Elgin did not really meant that, and I am convinced of it because otherwise it would be an insult to our farmers, to our farming community and indeed, to all Canadians.
So there will also be an advisory committee made up of representatives from all parts of the agricultural community, it will be placed under the direct authority of the Minister of Agriculture in order to ensure that the corporation's policies are consistent with the global Canadian strategy in matters of trade and production. Agriculture Canada will provide administrative services to this advisory committee which will include representatives besides those 1 mentioned a minute ago, from provincial governments, marketing boards, co-operatives, federal departments and services, the business community, farmers and consumers. I believe this wide range of representation will meet with the approval of my colleague from the other side, the hon. member for Joliette. As far as we are concerned, we have qualified people in our country.
Regarding the financial aspect, Mr. Speaker, Canagrex will be a Crown corporation established under Schedule C. it will have an annual budget appropriated by Parliament. The corporation will require a total investment of $12.3 million for its First three years of operation. It has been pointed out that the minister had said it would be a higher amount, and we now realize it will be only $12.3 million. I think the hon. member on this side who spoke before me has put it very aptly when he said you have to learn to walk before being able to run. Of course, during the first year, Canagrex will have to build up its structure. However, this corporation does not need a staff of 200 to run its operations. What we need is qualified people and I am sure we will have them. During the first year, only a few people will be enough to get the corporation going. Canagrex will establish a fund to which any benefit front joint ventures as well as loans or guarantees repaid to the corporation will be credited. Canagrex will deposit into this account all moneys paid to it as a result of joint ventures as well as reimbursements of loans and guaranties. Canagrex will be able to pay for its expenditures out of the financial transactions account.
When Canagrex is fully cost effective, it may borrow money from the Consolidated Revenue Fund. The contingent liabilities from the guarantees are limited to $75 million, of course. Certain limits will be provided for each loan, grant and loan guarantee. The due dates, the interest rates, the schedules for reimbursement and the other terms and conditions or applicable costs will also meet with the criteria for government programs or any other criterion authorized by the government.

Considering that it will take some time to make Canagrex operational and to hire the number of experts needed, it is imperative that we establish this corporation as soon as possible. Of course, Canagrex will operate under the new Crown Corporations Act providing that the said corporations will have to submit to the Treasury Board five-year plans which would be updated every year.
Furthermore, as far as the operation of the corporation is concerned, the advisory board will have to submit every year to the minister a marketing strategy for the next three years. The board will define its strategy on the basis of data provided by Agriculture Canada, the Department of International Trade, the provinces, and by the agricultural industry and private industry. That amalgamation of a variety of general data and interests will allow for the development of a practical and enlightened strategy. Canagrex should normally strive to develop foreign markets as well as new and existing agri-food products. I also heard earlier the hon. member for Prince Albert say that we should have new products. I think we shall begin with those we have. I indicated earlier a great number of products that we can export on the international market as early as tomorrow even if-and I commend them for that- pork processors are already exporting to the United States and supplying the very large Japanese market. This does not mean that at a given time they will not be pleased to have an organization such as Canagrex help them on the international market where conditions are sometimes very difficult, and I had the opportunity to discuss this matter with them.
Each year, the directors of Canagrex shall prepare a three-year corporate plan. The plan shall set forth its purposes and objectives, its target markets as well as the products to be dealt with in the years covered by the plan. The whole plan once approved will serve as a basis for the preparation of the annual operating and capital budget that Canagrex shall submit to the Minister of Agriculture for Treasury Board approval. In fact, Canagrex shall have to show through studies and other analyses that the projects proposed in the yearly plans are economically feasible and are likely to become profitable within a reasonable period of time. Finally, each year, the board of directors shall make a report on its activities which the minister will table in Parliament.
Therefore, Mr. Speaker, with all the provisions included in Bill C-85, as a Member of Parliament representing a rural riding where agriculture is of the utmost importance, where processing plants are on the increase, where agriculture is most diversified, I am convinced that Canagrex will make a most valuable contribution to the Canadian agricultural sector and processing industry. As I said a minute ago, this is an over view of this structure, Mr. Speaker, and I hope members opposite will not delay their approval of this bill which, once again, as I said earlier, will enhance the role of Canadian agriculture. I should like to end my remarks with these words, Mr. Speaker. The people in the Middle East are often referred
Canagrex Act
to as the oil-rich Arabs. 1 say that Canadians, in the 1980s, will be the Arabs of agriculture and agri-food products.

Mr. Speaker, it seems to me the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) has already made a speech. 1 would like to ask the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) to take part in this debate, and he would, of course, have an opportunity to speak for the Minister of Agriculture on the comments made earlier by my hon. colleague.
Mr. Speaker, I want to make a few comments and I was hoping that the mood would be a little less aggressive than it

January 27, 1982
Canagrex Act
was yesterday evening-after all, no one day is the same. However, bills and debates do not seem to change. On the other side of the House I sense great enthusiasm for this proposal to establish a Crown corporation for the export of agricultural products. I believe there is no problem as to the principle. In times like these, and in view of the problems with which our producers are faced, 1 feel there should be no objection to adding a new instrument for agricultural development to those that already exist, or to having a mechanism for promoting exports of our agricultural products. However, although we have no basic objection to this new concept, I do have some reservations because it is a new organizational structure, and because we do not know exactly what this other new structure is the government announced recently, which is based on the concept of reorganizing the country's economic development by consolidating the Department of Regional Economic Expansion and the Department of Industry, Trade and Commerce, while the Department of External Affairs is also involved-some ministers are going down a few notches while others may not be getting anything out of the new structure, I am not quite sure about this and in any case we do not know what exactly is involved.
The Prime Minister himself (Mr. Trudeau) had a lot of trouble explaining on television what this new economic development tool was supposed to be. In any case, it seems that the government intends to set up a rather extraordinary organization. Since we do not know exactly what the role of the new organization will be, the question arises whether the Crown corporation we are discussing could not have been integrated into this larger organization. With many other colleagues on this side of the House, I feel that when the bill is considered in committee, we will be able to have a far better idea of what is involved than we can from a short press release and a few understandably enthusiastic comments by government members.
This reservation is necessary, I believe, with respect to the importance that will be given to and the cost involved in this new economic development structure which, besides, seems to bring about a fundamental change in the role played by the Department of External Affairs. When considering the legislation in committee, we will be in a position, on this side of the House anyway, to ask relevant questions, because there should be some kind of relationship when we deal with economic development; agriculture cannot be totally set apart, and it is important for us, it is important for Quebec as well as for my riding. The minister has left the House for a few minutes, and 1 wanted to thank him for honouring me with his presence, not too long ago, in my riding. The Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Ostiguy) for one has stated that he had been in my riding some time ago to meet with a few producers. This made me wonder all of a sudden about what was happening, last summer, because I had so many visits, Mr. Speaker. I represent a rural riding and agriculture seems to
concern more people than ever, but those were very short visits. I will not go any further into this, Mr. Speaker.
In my riding, of course, there are many producers who will be interested in any proposal likely to promote our agricultural markets. Dairy producers are important in our area, as well as farmers involved in the production of fruits, vegetables, potatoes, pork, eggs, chicken and so on. Let us hope that maple syrup producers, for instance, will be able to sell their products through this new agency. It would be a good thing to see those producers who presently have big problems take advantage of this agency once it is in operation.
The second reservation 1 wanted to make right now, Mr. Speaker, is that the minister had a much broader idea in mind than what the Parliamentary Secretary explained to us today. According to the minister, some $60 million would be necessary to create this agency, which could give employment to 120 or 125 people, I think. Of course, there seemed to be a relation between the importance of this new corporation and the number of employees and the budget it would require. The hon. member for Chicoutimi (Mr. Dionne) feels sorry that this legislation has been introduced so late, but it is certainly not our fault. 1 think this time we did not hold up the introduction of this bill. Apparently the minister intended to introduce this piece of legislation 11 months ago and at that time the budget and the number of employees would have been greater than provided for in this legislation. Here we are dealing with $12 million and four or five employees. Then I wonder whether the Parliamentary Secretary to the Minister of Agriculture stated all the truth when he told us that for the first year Canagrex would be a rather modest operation, or rather whether the minister could not get the credits he wanted from the cabinet. Indeed, it would not have been the first time that the Minister of Agriculture had failed to obtain what he needed to promote the industry he represents, namely agriculture. Nevertheless, we are still skeptical when we hear the government talk about such an enormous over-all plan, not to say too costly. For the time being, I do not have to wonder about that, but only about the fact that this plan could be reduced so drastically from what it was in the original proposals.
1 certainly think that interesting and pertinent questions will be asked before our committee on agriculture. Earlier, 1 listened to the hon. member for Chicoutimi who said he was sorry that the passing of this legislation had been delayed for so long and that high interest rates made it very hard to build up inventories of agricultural products, especially where beef is concerned, and that it was much more difficult now to build up inventories than it used to be some months or some years ago because of interest costs. Such a criticism does not come from the opposition side but from a member on the government side, the hon. member for Chicoutimi, and I was happy to hear it because it confirms what we have been saying for at least the past year.

Some mention has been made-and I agree one hundred per cent-of the self-discipline that farmers have managed to show in some areas of production. More and more, they will run their business with the same discipline as that of any industrial manager. There is no doubt about that. I think that producers have demonstrated a lot of interest and compliance in agreeing to all these plans which today allow us a better control over our production in relation to our market needs. This is the only way to go. It is also relevant to emphasize the importance of food production on a global scale and to note our country's ability to meet this ever-increasing demand which, incidentally, will give our producers the opportunity to increase their incomes. I repeat, any proposition concerned with the promotion of this objective is worth consideration.
It has been said that this corporation will not replace existing agencies such as the Canadian Dairy Commission, the Canadian Wheat Board or other marketing boards, but the minister also said in his speech that if they ever needed help from this corporation they would be welcome to it. At this stage, it is not intended to act as a substitute for existing agencies but should the need arise, it could help them out. 1 think that when this bill goes through the committee stage, the minister will be asked some pretty interesting questions. Promoting the export of our agricultural products and increasing our exportations is certainly a worthy aim which all hon. members should support. I repeat that there appears to be a consensus as far as the principle is concerned.
In view of the present problems of our producers, I believe that any positive action to promote ever better agricultural production will always be well received on this side of the House, because I do not think, as you must understand, Mr. Speaker, that the recent budget can help our agriculture to start on the road to recovery. We are well aware, and other members have emphasized this before me, of the difficulties now facing our farmers. I know quite well, for instance, that the Minister of Agriculture tried to get much more money to bolster the Farm Credit Fund than he was able to obtain at this time.
We know that the farmers are extremely discouraged by the budget proposals. I therefore take this opportunity to remind the minister of the difficulties facing the farmers. He must understand that a sustained effort must be made for the farmers and those in difficulty. Of course, I shall be told that the budget includes a proposal to save those who are already going under, but they will not be saved completely. There is nothing to protect those who will go under in a short time. Those members who are at least interested in farming and who live in rural constituencies are also aware of the difficulties facing many other sectors such as hog producers and dairy farmers. The hon. member for Saint-Hyacinthe (Mr. Ostiguy) mentioned the problems faced by these producers in 1973, and which I recall quite well. There is also room for improvement

in other areas, and I say once again that any worth-while measure will be well received.
If 1 may, Mr. Speaker, I would like to say a few words about the board of directors. It appears that there will be 11 directors under the responsibility of the minister, of course, and that seven will be selected outside the public service. I do not know if ability will come before political stripe, as this is not written in the bill. The parliamentary secretary expressed concern earlier about the comments made by my colleague, the hon. member for Elgin (Mr. Wise), to the effect that there were not enough qualified people to-

1 think 1 can explain why my colleague said that. He is concerned about the level of competence of the directors because he does feel, as I do, that the people to be appointed to the board will probably be bosom friends of those in power. That explains his concern.
How could you imagine such a thing?

Furthermore, if 1 understood him correctly, the minister gave me the assurance that people from both political stripes would be appointed to the executive committee. We will make sure of that. Also provincial representatives of the business community and farm organizations will sit on the advisory committee. I do not know if all provinces will be represented on it. Naturally, I hope so, and I would like the minister to realize the importance of provincial representation.
I think it is important to have a dialogue with all the provinces, including the province of Quebec, and that the business community participate in those negotiations, in those consultations with farm organizations. In that respect, 1 would be pleased to hear in committee, which organizations the minister intends to have represented on the advisory committee.
I think those representatives should be chosen very carefully, since this corporation will have the responsibility of promoting our agriculture as well as our farm products abroad. Understandably, those people must be picked very carefully and board and advisory committee members should be selected on the basis of their skills and their experience in agriculture. And I shall insist on the presence and representation of the provinces. As the minister is probably aware, there is a tendency to emphasize the federal presence or even to centralize when all the provinces are concerned. I hope that this corporation will respect the provinces and provincial priorities as concerns their farm legislation. I hope that all other federal departments will follow suit, since such dialogue, negotiation and consultation with the provinces is essential in such a crucial area as agriculture.
Those were the few remarks I wished to make, Mr. Speaker, regarding that new corporation which has, I think, a most significant mandate. It will be much easier to consider such a bill in detail in committee. Certainly it will be easier to get

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is an auspicious day for Canadian agriculture and trade as we meet for second reading of the legislation that would bring Canagrex, the Canadian Agricultural Export Corporation, into being. I should like to commend the Minister of Agriculture (Mr. Whelan) for his efforts in promoting this corporation and for his expediency in introducing this legislation to establish Canagrex. 1 want to point out that over and above the 50 or more accomplishments to his credit which the Minister of Supply and Services (Mr. Blais) wanted to read into the record, we will soon be able to add this important piece of legislation to his achievements as Minister of Agriculture.
[DOT]	(1740)
The bill we are considering fulfils in large part the government's promise of developing the same reputation in markets for all Canadian agricultural products which this country enjoys in grain handling. It is also consistent with many of the recommendations made in the agri-food discussion paper "Challenge for Growth" which has clearly identified the need to supply and develop markets for all our agri-food products. Moreover, the international climate is ripe for Canada to take on a more active role in promoting the sale of its food products abroad.
As we enter the third year of this decade, it is becoming more clear all the time that the eighties have all the makings of becoming the decade of food production, much as the 1970s were known as the energy years.
Worldwide demand for food will have serious political, social and economic repercussions unless nations such as Canada, one of the four net exporting nations of food products, are able to boost food supplies.
World population is increasing by 75 million to 80 million per year, and food production will most likely not keep pace with this increase in world population. Canada must take on the challenge of expanding its food production to meet world demand, not only for its own sake but also as a responsibility toward those countries that depend on the exporting nations to feed their people. Food is, after all, man's most basic need and unless exporting nations capitalize on their potential to produce and export food products and understand more fully the requirements of each country, they risk triggering a crisis that is far worse than the energy crisis we knew.
Agri-food is the natural resource that offers the most hope for mankind and, as far as Canada is concerned, we have much to gain by developing this resource, because not only is it renewable but the agri-food industry has the potential for tremendous expansion. Optimistic estimates indicate that Canada will be able to increase its food production by two thirds in the next two decades. If we can develop the market for our agri-food products and meet wheat export targets of 36 million tonnes by 1990, agriculture may become the cornerstone of our economy. We will not only have expanded our agricultural base, but will have diversified it as well by opening new markets for products that have never in the past been competitive internationally.
At a Financial Post conference on agri-business in Toronto last fall, one participant predicted that if world population grew as predicted, Canadian food producers may have to supply 80 million new customers every year. However, in order to meet future demand, we require a thorough understanding on overview of world markets, a strategy to supply those markets, and the ability to do so comprehensively and consistently. Canagrex can make a big difference, serving as the focal point for various agricultural marketing efforts with the capacity to carry through on the long-term, higher-risk ventures.
Extensive discussions, analysis and a sense of commitment to improving Canada's export capability and track record have brought us to this stage today. It has been a lengthy but a worth-while process.
The idea of forming such a Crown corporation was first discussed by the Minister of Agriculture and representatives of farm organizations in 1978.
Canagrex has been widely discussed across Canada since the announcement of its planned formation in the Speech from the Throne in April, 1980. Comments from all sectors of the food and agriculture industry have been favourable. This is significant because Canagrex is expected to work closely with all sectors of the industry, including private firms, co-operatives, marketing boards, and individuals, to reinforce the export capability of the food and agriculture industry.
January 27, 1982

It should be borne in mind that the government, through Canagrex, wishes to encourage additional exports, not to duplicate the existing efforts of firms presently doing a good job. But Canagrex would have a necessary and important role as a co-ordinator of marketing thrusts across the country.
Canagrex will enable us to consolidate and intensify our efforts much more than we have in the past. This is essential if we wish to live up to our potential in food production. Canadians consume only part of our food production, and unless a serious attempt is made at selling these products abroad, the industry at home will never have the opportunity to grow.
By establishing an agricultural export corporation, we will develop an expertise we have never known in agri-food production and marketing. It goes without saying that if the agri-food sector is strong, then research in this area will also increase and improve. Furthermore, input into Canagrex will come from the business community, farm organizations and government, so that it represents the interests of all parties who have a part to play in agri-food production.
Support for Canagrex is strong across the country. On numerous occasions, there has been unanimous support for its creation by provincial ministers of agriculture. The farming community, too, favours the establishment of Canagrex. Farm organizations such as the Canadian Federation of Agriculture and the National Farmers Union, have repeatedly called for an agricultural export corporation. As well, a number of private companies and industry groups have expressed interest and support for a stronger federal role in agricultural export efforts. This of course, Mr. Speaker, is not surprising given that a better export capability for food and agricultural products will, in turn, facilitate an expansion of Canadian agricultural production and increase to the industry.
If Canada is to put more emphasis on trade, one of our first responsibilities should be to focus on areas of strength, and agriculture is no doubt at the top of the list. There is nothing unusual about the establishment of a Crown trading corporation.
Industrialized nations have come to realize that in order to compete more effectively in world markets, they must co-ordinate or even centralize their activities. The Canadian government has taken such an initiative in other sectors in order to improve trade relations with other countries by establishing, for instance, the Canada Development Corporation, the Export Development Corporation, the Canadian Commercial Corporation and even Petro-Canada.
It is already a known fact that many countries prefer or even insist on negotiating trade deals with governments of other countries either directly or through Crown corporations or government agencies. This is especially so in commercial relations with east European countries and with the developing countries. We may reach the point, if we have not already done so, that the success of our trade relations with the east and the Third World will depend on how much interest the government has in the corporation that is doing the trading. For example, in 1973, when the Hon. Donald Macdonald attempted to negotiate a deal with the Venezuelan government, the latter specified that it was prepared to sign a deal with the Canadian Crown corporation, but not if a private oil
Canagrex Act
company was involved. There are many other instances where countries have either hesitated or refused to sign deals with Canada, unless it was under the auspices of a Crown corporation. This has been a feature when signing energy deals with other countries such as with Mexico. The trend is likely to continue, especially when it concerns exports which are vital to human subsistence, such as food products.
Private industry itself has begun to recognize the importance of Crown corporations and government agencies in opening markets and in promoting and selling their products abroad. Rather than viewing these corporations as competitors, they have accepted them as important allies and partners in export markets. Canagrex will not only demonstrate the federal leadership that has been called for, but it will help to develop the agricultural potential which exists in all provinces to produce and market abroad more raw and processed food and agricultural products.
In addition to helping develop a firmer partnership between industry and government in marketing, Canagrex will act as a unifying force in Canada. It is conceivable that we may have missed significant trade opportunities in the past, opportunities that we may have taken more advantage of if Canagrex had been in place. For example, it is possible that our exports of seed potatoes to Portugal would have been enhanced through a joint venture involving Canagrex. Algeria has indicated that it would prefer to deal with an organization such as Canagrex for importing a number of agricultural commodities. A potential sale of livestock to Spain was lost because we could not match the terms and conditions offered by our competitors. Canagrex will be more attuned to the market requirements of a wide array of countries and products. Very simply, we cannot knock on doors unless we can deliver. Without Canagrex we have not been able to market our products as aggressively as world competition demands and as we could have done and will be able to do with Canagrex in place.
Our agricultural trade missions to such places as Egypt have been fruitful, but we have not been able to conclude significant deals without an organization in place to carry through with providing the link between industry and government to deliver the goods. Therefore, it is clear that the legislation with which we are dealing today and its adoption by the House will have a great impact upon Canada's ability to improve its balance of trade, its marketing efficiency and its role as a provider of food to a growing world population.
Canagrex enjoys considerable support outside the House. I would sincerely hope that it would continue to enjoy similar support from hon. members today. Members have already indicated an appreciation for what Canagrex has to offer when they waived the traditional waiting period to give unanimous approval for first reading of Bill C-85. For years we have seen export sales opportunities slip through our fingers because there was not a mechanism in place to provide the help needed to close deals on the scale involved. With the support of hon. members, such losses can now be a thing of the past. I urge every hon. member to approve this bill without delay.

Hear, hear!
